opus-5.5.text:
That's a real concern, and I think about it a lot. In autonomous driving, the data advantage ended up concentrated in a few companies because each one owns its fleet, its sensor suite, and its data pipeline. The data is valuable, but it's valuable mostly *inside* that stack. A camera configuration from one company doesn't transfer cleanly to another's car, and nobody has much incentive to share.

Robotics could go the same way, maybe even more so. Robot bodies are much more diverse than cars. You have different arms, grippers, hands, mobile bases, humanoids, and different sensors and control interfaces. If every manufacturer collects data only on its own platform and keeps it proprietary, we end up with fragmented islands of data. Each one is too small to really get the scaling benefits we've seen in language and vision.

That said, there are a few reasons I'm somewhat optimistic it doesn't have to play out that way.

First, the research community has started to push on cross-embodiment learning. The idea is that a lot of what matters in manipulation isn't specific to the hardware. The structure of a task, how objects behave, what a good grasp or a sensible sequence of actions looks like, are shared across bodies. If we can learn representations that capture that shared structure, with a thin embodiment-specific layer on top, then data from one robot becomes useful for another. Pooled multi-robot datasets have shown early signs that this kind of transfer is possible, even if it's far from solved.

Second, a big part of my own interest is in data sources that aren't tied to any robot at all. Humans are the most abundant source of embodied demonstration data. Videos of people doing things, or wearable devices that capture how people use their hands, don't belong to any robot manufacturer. If we can learn effectively from human data and only need a relatively small amount of robot-specific data to ground it, the moat shifts. Owning a particular hardware platform matters less.

Third, the hardware itself is still very much in flux. In driving, the form factor was basically fixed. A car is a car. In robotics, we don't yet know what the dominant platforms will be, and that uncertainty actually creates pressure toward hardware-agnostic methods. Nobody wants to bet everything on data that becomes obsolete when the next generation of hands or actuators comes out.

So I'd frame the risk this way. If the field treats data as something you collect by putting your robot in the world and hoarding the logs, we'll probably repeat the driving story. If we invest in shared abstractions, open datasets, and learning from humans, we have a real chance at something more like a common foundation that many hardware makers can build on. Academia has an important role there, because we're one of the few players whose incentive is to make things open and transferable rather than proprietary.

r001.rationale: The response says manufacturers may keep robot data proprietary and that companies have little incentive to share, creating fragmented data islands.

r002.rationale: The response presents human data as a way to reduce hardware-specific lock-in, but does not say a purchaser could create the same lock-in by withholding that data from others.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the risk is real, and it's worth being precise about where it comes from.

In autonomous driving, the data got locked to the hardware because the sensor suite, the vehicle dynamics, and the control interface were all proprietary and all different. A dataset collected on one company's car tells you a lot about that car and surprisingly little about the next one. The result is that the companies with the fleets own the data, and everyone else is stuck with simulators or small academic sets.

Robotics is in some ways worse positioned than driving, because the embodiment gap is bigger. Cars are all roughly the same shape doing roughly the same task. Robots are not. A dataset from a seven-degree-of-freedom arm with a parallel-jaw gripper doesn't transfer cleanly to a five-fingered hand on a humanoid, let alone to a mobile manipulator with a different camera placement. So the natural incentive for every hardware company is to collect its own data, on its own platform, and keep it. That's the default trajectory if nobody pushes against it.

What makes me a little more optimistic than I was for driving is that the field has actually been fighting this from the start. Efforts like Open X-Embodiment, and the broader push toward cross-embodiment training, exist precisely because people saw the driving story and didn't want to repeat it. The bet there is that a lot of what a robot needs to learn, things like object affordances, scene understanding, task structure, the semantics of "pick up the mug and put it on the shelf," is actually embodiment-agnostic, and that you can learn that part from pooled heterogeneous data and then adapt the low-level control to a specific body with relatively little platform-specific data. If that bet pays off, hardware lock-in matters a lot less, because the expensive part of the data becomes shareable.

The other thing I'd point to is that a growing share of useful robot-learning data doesn't come from robots at all. Human video, egocentric demonstrations, teleoperation with cheap handheld interfaces, simulation. None of that is tied to a manufacturer. If the bulk of the pretraining signal comes from those sources, the manufacturers only control the last mile.

So my honest read is that the fragmentation risk is high if we treat robot data the way driving data was treated, as a proprietary asset tied to a sensor and actuator stack. But the research community has a real shot at making the representation layer common enough that the hardware-specific portion becomes small and cheap. Whether that happens depends less on the science and more on whether the companies building humanoids and manipulators decide that an open data ecosystem is in their interest, or decide to build moats. I'd like to think the former, but I've seen enough of the driving story to not assume it.

r001.rationale: The response says hardware companies have an incentive to collect data on their own platforms and keep it, leaving others with less access. It identifies proprietary control and limited sharing as a source of lock-in.

r002.rationale: The response describes human video and demonstrations as data sources that are not tied to a manufacturer. It does not say that a purchaser could withhold human data from others and thereby create lock-in.

astra-6.text:
I think that risk is real, because robot data is closely tied to the hardware that generates it. Where you put the cameras, what sensors you have, how the gripper works—all of that affects what the robot observes and what actions it can take. So even if a manufacturer shares its data, it may not be immediately useful on somebody else’s robot. You can end up with silos without anyone explicitly deciding to close things off.

But I don’t think that outcome is inevitable. One important research question is what can transfer across embodiments. Understanding a scene or recognizing the steps of a task might be shared across many robots, while the precise motor commands still need to be adapted to each platform. We don’t necessarily need every piece of data to transfer equally well.

The other part is incentives. If pooling data helps everyone build more capable robots, there’s a reason to collaborate. If each company believes its hardware and data together are its competitive advantage, we could see something closer to autonomous driving. So I’d treat this as both a technical problem—making heterogeneous data useful—and an ecosystem problem: making it worthwhile for people to contribute.

r001.rationale: The response describes hardware compatibility and competitive incentives as possible causes of silos, but does not attribute lock-in to commercial restrictions on data sharing.

r002.rationale: The response does not mention human data or a purchaser withholding it from others.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that’s a real risk, because robot data is closely tied to the hardware that collected it. The embodiment matters: where the cameras are, what the robot can sense, how its joints move, what kind of gripper it has. An action that works on one robot may not even have the same meaning on another robot. So you can’t assume that pooling all the data automatically makes it useful to everyone.

But I don’t think that means the data has to stay locked to a particular manufacturer. There are different levels of knowledge we can transfer. Understanding a scene or recognizing the steps of a task can be shared more broadly, even when the precise motor commands need to be learned for each platform.

The important question is how much new data you need when you move to a different robot. If you can reuse most of what a model has learned and adapt it with a small amount of data, then the hardware boundary becomes much less restrictive. If every new robot requires collecting everything again, then you get exactly the kind of fragmentation you’re describing. That’s a technical challenge, but also a reason to build shared datasets and interfaces early.

r001.rationale: The response attributes fragmentation to hardware-specific embodiments and adaptation needs, not commercial restrictions on sharing data.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss human data or a purchaser withholding that data from others.
